rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She counts five past and twenty-nine present Qur’anic forms of bāʾ-wāw-hamza, generally figurative for bearing divine favor, anger, or sin; the relevant sense is settling, with a related occurrence in al-Tawba.
rows.anchor: ومن الثلاثى (باء) جاء الفعل ماضيا خمس مرات، ومضارعْا (تبوء) تسعًا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, tabawwaʾa means to settle or reside; al-mabāʾa is a home, while bāʾa bi-dhanb means to acknowledge and assume a sin or blood-guilt.
rows.anchor: وفي اللغة: تبوأ المكانَ حلَّه وأقام، والمباءة المنزل كالبيئة، وبيت النحل فى الجبل

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda glosses tabawwiʾu al-muʾminīn as preparing a place for them; al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān give a similar explanation.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة فى المجاز: متخذا لهم مضاف، ونحوه فى تفسير القرطبي وأبى حيان

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari transmits ʿUmar’s counsel that the caliph safeguard the rights of the early Emigrants and accept the good of the Helpers who settled in the abode and faith before the Prophet’s migration, forgiving their faults.
rows.anchor: أخرج عن عمر رضى الله عنه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also explains al-ṣarīm as something gone, supporting the sense with a poetic usage.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: كالذاهب. واستشهد له بقول الشاعر

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reads the orchard as having become like a black night.
rows.anchor: مثل ما قاله الفراء في معنى الآية: كاليل الأسود

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba says it became black as night; night and day are each called ṣarīm because each breaks away from the other.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة في تأويل المشكل: أي سوداء كالليل لأن الليل ينصرم عن النهار، والنهار ينصرم عن الليل

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nābigha’s verse is cited as evidence that Arabs used the related aṣrām in a simile of dark night.
rows.anchor: نعم أما سمعت بقول النابغة وهو يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One oath-form attributed to believers entails expiation when they have sworn.
rows.anchor: وجاء الفعل مرة واحدة مسنداً إلى ضمير الذين آمنوا فوجبت عليهم كفارة الحلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses qasam for truthful oaths, calls one oath great, poses an oath as a question for reflection, and invokes it in the solemn testimony procedure for a bequest.
rows.anchor: وأما القسم، فيأتي في الإيمان الصادقة: وجاء موصوفاً بالعظمة في آية الواقعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden owners’ oath in Sūrat al-Qalam is presented as sincere.
rows.anchor: وكان أصحاب الجنة، في سورة القلم، صادقين:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When wrongdoers swear at the Resurrection that they remained only an hour, the author says they are not lying.
rows.anchor: وليس المجرمون بكاذبين إذ يقسمون يوم تقوم الساعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an also attributes oaths to the misguided, arising from delusion or an appearance of sincerity before their error is exposed.
rows.anchor: وكذلك يسند القسم في القرآن إلى الضالين، عن وهم منهم أو إيهام بالصدق، قبل أن ينكشف أنهم كانوا على ضلال

rows.speaker: الأصمعي وأبو حاتم السجستاني
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī takes al-ṣarīm as night; Abū Ḥātim says it can be night or day as either parts from the other, and can also mean something cut off.
rows.anchor: ذكره الأصمعي في (الأضداد) وقال: ومن الصريم الليل قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الشيباني
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī cites Zuhayr’s verse to support the interpretation of ṣarīm as night.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي عمرو الشيباني، وأنشد بيت زهير: يريد الليل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī transmits Ibn ʿAbbās’s explanations: dark night and, in another report, black ash.
rows.anchor: وأسند الطبري عن ابن عباس، قال: الليل المظلم. وعنه أيضاً: كالرماد الأسود

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān interprets the orchard as harvested crop, taking ṣarīm to mean something cut down.
rows.anchor: وعن سفيان: كالزرع المحصود، فالصريم بمعنى المصروم

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib relates ṣarm to severance and gives two readings: trees stripped of their fruit or trees blackened as if by burning; Ibn al-Athīr likewise glosses it as cutting.
rows.anchor: والراغب فسر الصرْم بالقطيعة. وقال في الآية: قيل: أصبحت كالأشجار الصريمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She prefers the cutting or harvesting sense over ‘gone’: the context does not support swearing to make the garden disappear and finding it like something gone.
rows.anchor: ونرى دلالة القطع في الصرم. وفي الهجر والقطيعة، وفي الصرم: البت، والصارم: القاطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the common view that oath-wāw serves only to magnify what is sworn by, she reads it as a rhetorical signal directing attention to perceptible realities that cannot be disputed, preparing for disputed abstractions or unseen truths.
rows.anchor: هو أن هذه الواو قد خرجت عن أصل معناها اللغوي الأول في القسم للتعظيم، إلى معنى بلاغي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Oaths by dawn, sun, and night use physical degrees of light and darkness to clarify guidance and truth or error and falsehood, as does the Qur’an’s figurative use of light and darkness.
rows.anchor: يَجلو معاني من الهدى والحق أو الضلال والباطل، بماديات من النور والظلمة في مختلف درجاتهما

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī explains that a sūra mentioning the Qur’an thereby draws attention to all of it; other opening forms suit hearts not occupied by anything besides the Qur’an, and the openings of al-Ḥajj and al-Taḥrīm invoke great matters.
rows.anchor: وقد رد الرازي على الأول، بأن السورة التي فيها ذكر القرآن

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī attributes the absence of a later Qur’an reference in some letter-opened sūras to the weight of the Qur’an’s obligations and meanings.
rows.anchor: وأما السور التي افتتحت بالحروف ولم يذكر بعدها القرآن أو التنزيل، فعلَّله بأن ثقل القرآن، بما فيه من التكاليف والمعاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds al-Rāzī’s explanations unconvincing and plainly forced.
rows.anchor: ولا يبدو ردهُّ مقنعاً، بل هو واضح التكلف

rows.speaker: الزركشي
rows.claim: Al-Zarkashī notes the usual pattern of mentioning the Qur’an after disjoint letters and asks why al-ʿAnkabūt and al-Rūm differ.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن عادة القرآن العظيم في ذكر هذه الحروف، أن يذكر بعدها ما يتعلق بالقرآن

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr’s inductive answer is that every sūra opened with disjoint letters includes a defense of the Qur’an and a demonstration of its inimitability.
rows.anchor: فهداه الاستقراء إلى أن كل سورة افتتحت بالحروف فلابد أن يذكر فيها الانتصار للقرآن وبيان إعجازه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wāw normally links clauses, but as an oath it comes first to authenticate what is denied or to mark acknowledgment and testimony.
rows.anchor: والأصل في الواو أن تأتي في درَج الكلام للربط والعطف، فإذا جاءت للقسم فإن لها الصدارة

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Most exegetes take oath-wāw as magnifying the object sworn by and seek the source of its greatness.
rows.anchor: وقد اتجه بها المفسرون، أو جمهرتهم فيما أعلم، إلى تعظيم المقسَم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She argues that perceiving a purpose in a created thing does not establish its greatness, and that exegetes often overlook restrictions such as ‘when it settles’ or ‘when it falls.’
rows.anchor: وأكثر ما ذكروه من ذلك يدخل في الحكمة وهي تختلف تماماً عن العظمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She argues that interpreters often overlook the qualifiers attached to the objects of the oath.
rows.anchor: ثم إنهم غالباً، لم يراعوا القيد في المقسم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She objects that interpreters discuss night in general while the verse restricts it to the condition ‘when it settles.’
rows.anchor: وفي الليل إذا سجى، تحدثوا عن عظمة الليل مطلق الليل، وهو في الآية مقيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She points out that interpreters praise daylight in general even though the oath is limited to forenoon, when light may be weaker than at noon.
rows.anchor: ففي الضحى مثلاً تحدثوا عن عظمة الضياء، وليس مقصوراً على وقت الضحى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She questions the link between the supposed greatness of night and day and the claim that human striving differs, and between the falling star and the assertion that the Prophet is neither astray nor deluded.
rows.anchor: بين: إن سعيكم لشتى؟ أو بين عظمة النجم إذا هوى، و {مَا ضَلَّ صَاحِبُكُمْ وَمَا غَوَى} ؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She asks what rhetorical effect oath-wāw has and whether an Arab listener perceived a difference between that form and an explicit ‘I swear by’ construction.
rows.anchor: وبين مألوف التعبير بصريح القسم: أقسم بالضحى، وبالليل إذا سجى، وأقسم بالنجم إذا هوى؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She observes that sūras opening with oath-wāw are all Meccan; no Medinan sūra begins with it.
rows.anchor: وكلها سور مكية، ولم تأت سورة مدنية مبدوءة بهذه الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited account calls endings eloquent when they arise easily from the meaning, but rejects making the meaning follow a forced sound pattern; it cites matching endings in Ṭā Hā, al-Ṭūr, al-ʿĀdiyāt, and al-Fajr, including deletion of final yāʾ in the latter.
rows.anchor: يكون يأتي طوعاً سهلاً وتابعاً للمعاني، وبالضد من ذلك حتى يكون متكلفاً يتبعه المعنى

rows.speaker: الرماني
rows.claim: Al-Rummānī distinguishes matching endings, which he allows calling sajʿ, from merely near endings, but the author rejects his blanket claim that sajʿ is defective while Qur’anic fawāṣil are eloquent.
rows.anchor: فأما قول الرومانى: "إن السجع عيب والفواصل بلاغة" على الإطلاق، فغلط

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafājī suggests scholars called all Qur’anic endings fawāṣil, even when they rhyme, to keep the Qur’an from an associated description.
rows.anchor: وأظن أن الذي دعا اصحابنا إلى تسمية كل ما في القرآن فواصل، ولم يسموا ما تماثلت حروفه سجعاً

rows.speaker: الفخر الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī and al-Nīsābūrī count preserving the rhyme among the reasons the second-person kāf is omitted from ‘wa-mā qalā.’
rows.anchor: وعدّ "الفخر الرازي" من وجوه حذف الكاف رعاية الفاصلة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She rejects rhyme as the explanation: the sūra has no thāʾ-ending, and even contains no thāʾ, so a forced substitute for fa-ḥaddith would not fit a rhyme pattern.
rows.anchor: ولو كان البيان القرآني يتعلق بهذا الملحظ اللفظي فحسب، لما عدل عن رعاية الفاصلة في الآيات بعدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted kāf avoids directly telling the Prophet ‘you are hated’: qalā carries harsh senses of rejection and intense enmity, while waddʿa evokes a loving farewell and hoped-for return.
rows.anchor: تقتضيه حساسية مرهفة بالغة الدقة واللطف، هي ما تحاشى خطابه رسوله المصطفى، في موقف الإيناس، بصريح القول: وما قلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the later clauses, context already supplies the omitted addressee; stating the kāf would therefore be needless padding.
rows.anchor: وحُذفت كاف الخطاب في الفواصل بعدها، لأن السياق بعد ذلك أغنى عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses imtiḥān for hearts tested for piety and for believers’ examination of migrant women; ibtilāʾ appears once for guardians assessing orphans’ maturity and most often for God’s tests of servants.
rows.anchor: ومن الذين آمنوا للمهاجرات في آية الممتحنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She notes that ibtilāʾ also occurs in descriptions of the Last Day, and that fitna may come from God, Satan, magic, hypocrites, disbelievers, or people testing one another.
rows.anchor: وأما الفتنة فتكون من الله تعالى في مثل آيتى العنكبوت

rows.speaker: الراغب وابن الأثير
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib and Ibn al-Athīr say balāʾ and fitna are used more often and more clearly for hardship; the author says her survey supports this, though testing through prosperity also occurs and can be paired with adversity.
rows.anchor: وقول الراغب وابن الأثير، إن البلاء والفتنة أظهر في الشدة وأكثر استعمالا، يؤيده الاستقراء

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A prophetic report says people endured a test through adversity and will also be tested through prosperity.
rows.anchor: ومنه الحديث: "ابتليتم بفتنة الضراء فصبرتم، وستبتلون بفتنة السراء"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening horse-raid image recalls a familiar dawn attack that surprises people and scatters a group in dust, prefiguring the sudden, unseen Resurrection that catches the ungrateful unprepared and scatters people from their graves.
rows.anchor: السورة تبدأ بالواو لافتة إلى ما عهد القوم من غارات الخيل المصبحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath by Time evokes human beings being crushed and refined under pressure; Time extracts their essence and exposes their worth, explaining loss or salvation in the next verses.
rows.anchor: الواو في موضعها الذي تطرد به الظاهرة الأسلوبية في اللفت إلى ابتلاء الإنسان بالزمن يعصره ويصهره بالضغط والمعاناة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Best of judges’ and ‘wisest of judges’ acknowledge that people also judge; the Qur’an illustrates human judgment through commands to judge justly and accounts of David and Solomon judging a field.
rows.anchor: منظور فيها إلى أن الحكم قد يكون من المخلوقين

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib distinguishes God’s creation without a model from human making by a model; the author instead sees the form aḥsan as not straightforwardly derived from khalaqa / khāliq, but from the sense of khaliq (worthy).
rows.anchor: و"الراغب" في المفردات يفرق بين الخلق من الله على غير مثال، ومن الناس على مثال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A comparative is explicitly restricted by a specification such as azkā ṭaʿāman; bare superlatives are different unless the text states a criterion or comparison.
rows.anchor: والتقييد بوجه مفاضله، في أفعل التفضيل، إنما يتعين صراحة بالتمييز في مثل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She reads haḍīm as clustered or connected, using the poetic phrase ‘mahdūmat al-kashḥayn’ as a clue to compactness.
rows.anchor: تأويل هضيم في المسألة بانضمام، أو اتصال، بعضه ببعض

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the date clusters as ripened and mature.
rows.anchor: والطبري روى الآية من اختلاف أهل التأويل بإسناده عن ابن عباس، قال: أينع ونضج فهو هضيم

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Other interpreters take haḍīm as crushed or broken apart because of its softness and moisture.
rows.anchor: وعن آخرين: هو المتهشم المتفتت

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Another reported explanation is soft fresh dates that are easy to chew.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: هو من الرطب اللين تهصمه

rows.speaker: غيرهم
rows.claim: A further group understands the date clusters as overlapping one another.
rows.anchor: وقال غيرهم: الراكب بعضه بعضا

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers ‘broken by its softness and moisture’ as the soundest interpretation.
rows.anchor: وأولى الأقوال عنده بالصواب، أن الهضيم هو المتكسر من لينة ورطوبته

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib defines haḍm as crushing something soft and reads the fruit as packed one inside another, as if crushed.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب: الهضم شدخ ما فيه رخاوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She traces the senses to digestion: softness and easy digestion, delicate flanks, and metaphorical loss or injustice; she concludes that haḍīm suggests clustered palm fruit whose original softness makes it easy to eat.
rows.anchor: ولعلها ترجع فيها إلى هضم الطعام، والهضوم والهاضوم كل ما هضم طعاماً، وبملحظ منه جاء الهضم خمص البطن
